source_title: Breaking: Woman shot dead by police in Adelaide's east
source_excerpt:
Police at the scene of the shooting at Firle in Adelaide's east. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie )
A woman has been shot and killed by police in an incident at Firle in Adelaide's east.
Police said the woman was reportedly armed with an axe and that she threatened them upon their arrival in the early hours of this morning.
The Acting Police Commissioner says she had reviewed body-worn camera vision and was "confident the officers acted appropriately".
Police have shot and killed a 63-year-old woman who was reportedly armed with an axe during a confrontation at Firle in Adelaide's eastern suburbs.
The incident happened around 2am on Thursday morning, when police were called to Gwynne Street responding to reports "that a woman was armed with an axe".
"The initial call was that the person was violent and creating a disturbance and that they had an axe," Acting Police Commissioner Linda Williams said on Thursday afternoon.
Police said upon arrival, patrols were confronted by the woman, who allegedly threatened them with the axe in the front yard.
They said the woman was asked to drop the weapon but she refused before officers used a taser, which was ineffective.
Police alleged the woman continued to threaten officers and had struck one of them in the leg with the axe.
Acting Commissioner Williams said an officer then fired two shots that struck the woman.
"That situation escalated very fast," she said.
Major Crime Investigation Branch detectives and Forensic Response Section officers are at the scene. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie )
Officers attempted first aid before ambulance paramedics arrived, police said, but the woman died at the scene.
"Major Crime Investigation Branch detectives, Forensic Response Section officers and investigators from Internal Investigation Section are at the scene and will examine the circumstances surrounding the incident," police said.
Acting Police Commissioner Linda Williams said she had reviewed body-worn footage in the lead-up to and during the shooting and was "confident the officers acted appropriately".
"I'm very comfortable with the practices and the procedures and how police responded to a very difficult and a very challenging situation," she said.
The injured police officer was treated by paramedics at the scene for minor bruising to his leg.
A neighbour who knew the woman told 891 ABC Adelaide she was shocked to hear what had happened.
A neighbour says she has been left shocked and deeply saddened. ( ABC News )
She said the woman was "well known in Gwynne Street to have been lovely and [was] always asking how people are".
"There's never been any sign of any aggression or anything like that.
"It's very much of a shock to hear what has happened, but also my thoughts are with the SAPOL officer who had to make that very quick decision — so my thoughts are with them and hoping that they get a speedy physical and emotional recovery. Very sad."
Police were called to the scene about 2am. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie )
The neighbour said she was woken by loud bangs, and initially assumed it was "someone punching the laneway fence".
"Then my daughter came in and asked, 'Mum, did you just hear all that yelling?'" she said.
"I said, 'No, I just woke up to someone banging on the fence'. She said, 'No that sounded like gunshots'."
Another local who lives only a few doors down told 891 ABC Adelaide she did not know the woman but she was shocked nonetheless.
"She, I think, lived quite a reserved life. All I saw her doing really was gardening ... so it's very shocking to me, she seemed like quite a peaceful person," she said.
"I heard two loud bangs in the middle of the night," another local said.
Police said they would prepare a report for the coroner and a Commissioner's Inquiry would be conducted to examine whether SA Police policies and procedures were followed.
Derrick McManus, who survived being shot 14 times during a 1994 siege while serving as a STAR Group officer, said his sympathies went to the woman and her family.
Multiple police agencies have been at the scene. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie )
He said the mental health of the officers involved also need to be considered.
"Police training is to shoot to stop any imminent danger," he said.
"To shoot someone in the leg does not guarantee any negation of any threat, so the centre body mass is where we aim to stop the threat most effectively.
"The police involved will go through a major investigation, they will be interrogated for possibly hours immediately after this."
Police said a report would be prepared for the coroner. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie )
